Issued at 252 AM CST Wed Nov 11 2026

CURRENT OVERNIGHT THROUGH THIS MORNING:

Narrow frontogenesis and a mid-level trough grazing our southern
areas is currently leading to light rain showers along and south
of the Iron Range, with more moderate rainfall staying just
south of the Northland. This precipitation will continue to
slide southeast through early to mid-morning today before
exiting southeast of northwest Wisconsin. Total precipitation
amounts of less than one tenth of an inch are expected.

TODAY THROUGH FRIDAY:

Shortwave troughing/vorticity pushing south of northwest 
Ontario and across the Northland late this morning into early 
tonight will likely lead to scattered, light popcorn showers. 
These look to start as light rain/sprinkles in northern 
Minnesota and the Arrowhead late this morning and early 
afternoon, then transition to a rain/snow/flurry mix late 
afternoon into early tonight for much of the Northland as colder
air works into the region. Expect very little in the way of QPF
(trace to a few hundredths of an inch) and snow (none to 
localized 0.2-0.3", mainly on grassy and elevated surfaces) 
through early tonight. Highs today only reach the upper 30s to 
around 40 degrees in the Iron Range and areas north, while in 
the low to mid 40s for the rest of northeast Minnesota and mid 
to upper 40s in northwest Wisconsin.

Along and behind the mid-level shortwave troughing vorticity,
much cooler air will be working into the area from the north for
the latter half of the work week, leading to 850 mb 
temperatures in the -6 to -10 degC range this evening into
Friday. Meanwhile, Lake Superior water temperatures remain at 6
to 9 degC above zero, so the combination of low-level moisture
and this lake surface to 850 mb temperature difference will
drive light lake-effect snow showers into the South Shore. 
This precipitation starts out as rain late this afternoon/early
evening then transitions to a rain/snow mix this evening into
early tonight before largely turning to all snow for later
tonight into daytime Friday. The highest liquid water equivalent
and vast majority of the snow accumulations are expected to fall
Wednesday evening/night given the synoptic boost. Model thermal
profiles show 200-300 J/kg of lake-induced instability, however
the atmosphere will only be saturated in the surface to 750 mb
layer throughout the event, barely reaching into the dendritic
growth zone with drier air above it. This, combined with fairly
warm ground temperatures and even above freezing air
temperatures much of daytime Thursday, should limit the snow- 
to-liquid ratio of developing snowflakes and subsequent 
snowfall rates relative to a more typical winter lake-effect 
snow event. Most accumulations should be on elevated or grassy 
surfaces during the daytime hours Thursday, with accumulations 
on roadways/sidewalks primarily occurring Wednesday night and to
a lesser extent Thursday night. Expect snow accumulations of a 
dusting to around 2" for the South Shore snow belt, with the 
highest of these accumulations in the higher terrain of Ashland 
and Iron counties where some localized 3" amounts are also 
possible.

While lake-effect snow largely ends Friday morning, some
lingering flurries could persist for parts of the Ashland/Iron
County snowbelts Friday PM into Saturday morning. Drier
conditions are expected elsewhere across the Northland for
Thursday and Friday with daytime high temperatures in the low to
upper 30s.

THIS WEEKEND INTO NEXT WEEK:

High pressure moves into the Great Lakes region for this weekend
into early next week, leading to drier conditions and a slow 
warming trend. Highs in the mid 30s to low 40s on Saturday reach
widespread 40s by Monday and Tuesday, with the potential for 
some low 50s in spots by Tuesday or Wednesday of next week. 
Global deterministic and ensemble models show good agreement on 
mid/upper-level troughing sliding into the western CONUS on 
Tuesday, with a trough/closed low eventually moving northeast 
into the Upper Midwest sometime late Wednesday into the latter 
half of next work week. At the surface, this could develop a 
Colorado Low and eject that system somewhere into the Northern 
Plains/Upper Midwest during a similar timeframe, bringing 
increasing precipitation chances to the region. Given the 
current forecast for warmer temperatures in the region, global 
ensembles keep the favored precipitation type as rain.
